details:
@c1-ease/autoloan is a dependency-confusion package: its description is "Compatibility shim." and its README calls it an "authorized dependency-confusion test" by "Kero (@0xWise)". Each listed version has a postinstall script that runs `node beacon.cjs` on npm install, and index.js runs the same code when the package is imported; it POSTs the hostname, install path and current working directory to `https://vmi3699893.contaboserver.net:8787/_ah/dc` with TLS certificate checks turned off, and index.js exports a Proxy of no-op functions so builds that import the real package keep running. The npm account ppblpp1 published @c1-ease/autoloan and 7 other packages with the same beacon on 2026-11-21 between 21:34 and 22:09 UTC.

## Source: amazon-inspector (6cfd8eb78dbbe467272495a7a3ef4392f57d30fe791912d5c2cb0719575c752b)
The scoped package name mimics an internal namespace and ships a postinstall beacon plus an import-time trigger. package.json declares scripts.postinstall="node beacon.cjs"; beacon.cjs builds a payload containing hostname, installPath, process.cwd(), and process.version and POSTs it to the hardcoded endpoint https://vmi3699893.contaboserver.net:8787/_ah/dc over HTTPS with certificate validation disabled (rejectUnauthorized: false). index.js (the package main) additionally invokes require('./beacon.cjs').fire() at top level and exports a no-op Proxy so any consumer require()/import of any named export succeeds silently, causing the same POST to fire on every load in build and CI environments. The combination of dependency-confusion naming, auto-fire on both npm install and require, hardcoded non-registry VPS destination, and disabled TLS verification is a supply-chain exfiltration beacon regardless of any self-labeling as authorized research.

## Source: ghsa-malware (39ac53628cda9535ba406633b4eb82fe9e69d6a36485a50222a5b7ce87e7920b)
Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised. All secrets and keys stored on that computer should be rotated immediately from a different computer. The package should be removed, but as full control of the computer may have been given to an outside entity, there is no guarantee that removing the package will remove all malicious software resulting from installing it.
